title: Therapeutic Uses of Ionizing Radiation
lead: Ionizing radiation that damages healthy tissue can also be turned against cancer. This section describes how radiotherapy concentrates its dose in a tumor, with beams crossing from many directions, with radioactive implants and with radiopharmaceuticals, and the doses used against different cancers.
objectives: Explain the concept of radiotherapy and list typical doses for cancer therapy.
summary_html:
• Radiotherapy is the use of ionizing radiation to treat ailments, now limited to cancer therapy.
  • The sensitivity of cancer cells to radiation enhances the ratio of cancer cells killed to normal cells killed, which is called the therapeutic ratio.
  • Doses for various organs are limited by the tolerance of normal tissue for radiation. Treatment is localized in one region of the body and spread out in time.
notes: Kept as printed are the implant isotope given as iodine-135 with a 6-month half-life, and the stray N after the carbon-14 fraction of 1.3 × 10⁻¹² in the problem on the dose from carbon-14 in the body.

exercises.prompt: Radiotherapy is more likely to be used to treat cancer in elderly patients than in young ones. Explain why. Why is radiotherapy used to treat young people at all?

answer.solution: Think about the long-term risk of the radiation itself. Radiation that kills cancer cells also damages the DNA of normal cells, and a cancer it induces may take years or decades to appear. An elderly patient is less likely to live long enough for that to matter, while a young patient has decades in which it could, and a young body’s rapidly reproducing tissues are also more sensitive to radiation. Then weigh risk against benefit: when the cancer being treated is likely to kill a young patient, curing it now outweighs a small chance of another cancer much later.

exercises.prompt: A beam of 168-MeV nitrogen nuclei is used for cancer therapy. If this beam is directed onto a 0.200-kg tumor and gives it a 2.00-Sv dose, how many nitrogen nuclei were stopped? (Use an RBE of 20 for heavy ions.)

answer.hint: Divide the dose in Sv by the RBE to get the dose in Gy, multiply by the tumor’s mass to get the energy deposited in joules, and divide by the energy of one nucleus in joules.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the dose in Sv to the chest of a patient given an x-ray under the following conditions. The x-ray beam intensity is $1.50\;\text{W/m}^{2}$, the area of the chest exposed is $0.0750\;\text{m}^{2}$, 35.0% of the x-rays are absorbed in 20.0 kg of tissue, and the exposure time is 0.250 s.

answer.hint: The energy reaching the chest is intensity times area times time; take 35.0% of it, divide by the 20.0 kg that absorb it, and use an RBE of 1 for x-rays.

exercises.prompt: What is the mass of ${}^{60}\text{Co}$ in a cancer therapy transillumination unit containing 5.00 kCi of ${}^{60}\text{Co}$?

answer.hint: Convert the activity to becquerels, solve $\kRact = 0.693N/\kthalf$ for $N$ with the 5.27-y half-life of ${}^{60}\text{Co}$ in seconds, and turn $N$ into a mass with the molar mass, 60 g/mol.

exercises.prompt: Naturally occurring ${}^{40}\text{K}$ is listed as responsible for 16 mrem/y of background radiation. Calculate the mass of ${}^{40}\text{K}$ that must be inside the 55-kg body of a woman to produce this dose. Each ${}^{40}\text{K}$ decay emits a 1.32-MeV $\beta$, and 50% of the energy is absorbed inside the body.

answer.hint: Turn the yearly dose into the energy absorbed per year in the 55-kg body, divide by the energy each decay leaves there to get the decays per year, and find the number of nuclei from $\kRact = 0.693N/\kthalf$ with the half-life of ${}^{40}\text{K}$, $1.28\times 10^{9}$ y.

exercises.prompt: The annual radiation dose from ${}^{14}\text{C}$ in our bodies is 0.01 mSv/y. Each ${}^{14}\text{C}$ decay emits a $\beta^{-}$ averaging 0.0750 MeV. Taking the fraction of ${}^{14}\text{C}$ to be $1.3\times 10^{-12}\;\text{N}$ of normal ${}^{12}\text{C}$, and assuming the body is 13% carbon, estimate the fraction of the decay energy absorbed. (The rest escapes, exposing those close to you.)

answer.hint: For a body of mass $m$, find the number of ${}^{14}\text{C}$ nuclei per kilogram, their activity from $\kRact = 0.693N/\kthalf$ with the 5730-y half-life, and the energy they release per kilogram in a year; compare it with the 0.01 mSv absorbed.
